  • Can traditional methods help you conceive a boy?
Trying to Conceive

Can traditional methods help you conceive a boy?

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A plan promising a boy can be surprisingly detailed: particular nights, a list of foods for both partners, several teas and rules about what to do after sex. Detail can make a method feel dependable, but it does not establish that the method works. No reliable home routine has been shown to let a family choose a boy, and some of the proposed steps can add unnecessary risk or pressure.

Separate a personal hope from a medical claim

Some people have a preference about their future child’s sex, while others face expectations from relatives. A preference does not make an unsupported treatment effective. It is possible to acknowledge the feeling without accepting a seller’s promise or blaming either partner for the outcome.

Traditional practices can have cultural meaning. That is a different question from whether a practice reliably changes the chance of a male birth. A claim about effectiveness needs suitable research, including a comparison with what happens without the method.

What usually determines chromosomal sex

An egg typically carries an X chromosome, while a sperm typically carries either X or Y. In the usual pattern, the combination at fertilization contributes to sex development. There are variations in chromosomes and development, so this short explanation does not describe every person.

Neither partner consciously chooses which sperm fertilizes the egg. Food classifications, room arrangements and rules about which side to lie on do not give someone control over that event. A child’s sex is not a measure of a parent’s effort, worth or success in following a routine.

Seasons, weekdays and times of day

Some programmes prescribe winter or spring, certain weekdays or a time before dawn. These precise instructions are not evidence that the timing selects a boy. A routine can be repeated consistently and still have no demonstrated effect on the claimed outcome.

Timing in relation to ovulation is a separate issue. It can help identify days when pregnancy is possible, but a prospective study of intercourse timing did not find a practical way to choose infant sex. Restricting attempts to a supposedly lucky night may miss opportunities within a fertile window.

Fragrance and atmosphere are matters of preference

Flowers, saffron-like scents, perfume or incense may be presented as creating the right atmosphere or a “warming” environment. Enjoying a scent or feeling relaxed does not show that it changes which sperm fertilizes the egg. A pleasant experience is not a sex-selection result.

There is no need to buy a special room product or continue using one that causes discomfort. Choose an environment that both partners find comfortable. Do not interpret the absence of a prescribed fragrance as a reason a pregnancy did not occur or a child was not the hoped-for sex.

Positions, orgasm order and lying still

Instructions may involve lying on the right side, raising one side with bedding, deeper penetration, a particular orgasm sequence or remaining still afterward. None has an established role in selecting a boy. ASRM also finds no evidence that position or post-sex routines improve the chance of conception.

Comfort and agreement should guide sexual activity. Do not endure pain or turn orgasm into a requirement for a successful pregnancy. Normal movement afterward does not mean that someone has spoiled a chance to conceive the desired sex.

A food list is not a boy-conceiving prescription

Suggested menus often include meat, poultry, eggs, nuts, dried fruit, honey and spices such as cinnamon, ginger, cumin or saffron. Individual foods may fit a varied diet, but grouping them as “warming” does not demonstrate an effect on infant sex. Avoiding foods labelled “cooling” is not an established treatment either.

Neither partner needs a special combination of fruit, a large breakfast or a pre-sex coffee as a sex-selection step. There is no validated programme based on eating particular numbers of dates, chestnuts or apples. Choose meals for nourishment, enjoyment and any personal medical needs rather than a promised result.

Do not add salt or sugar to chase a result

Advice to eat sea salt before and after meals or deliberately choose salty foods should not be treated as proven fertility science. Sea salt still contributes sodium. Excess sodium can raise blood pressure, so calling the salt natural does not remove the health concern.

Sweet drinks, syrups and desserts likewise do not become fertility treatments because they are assigned to a particular menstrual day. A plan can be nutritionally unsuitable even when it includes familiar foods. There is no reason to increase salt or sweets to pursue an unproven sex-selection benefit.

Seeds, medicinal teas and herbal mixtures

Some routines propose seed preparations during menstruation, or repeated drinks containing herbs such as hops, lavender, ginger, chamomile, thyme, rosemary or nettle. Names associated with everyday food can make concentrated products seem automatically safe, although dose, plant part and preparation can differ substantially.

Herbal products may interact with medicines or contain variable ingredients, and many have little pregnancy-safety information. Culinary use is different from taking an extract or medicinal mixture. Show the complete label to a clinician or pharmacist rather than assuming a calendar-based course is safe because conception has not yet been confirmed.

Claims about herbs for the sperm-producing partner

Chicory and other herbal drinks are sometimes promoted as increasing semen volume or sperm numbers and therefore producing a boy. This combines two separate claims: an effect on semen, and an effect on infant sex. Even a genuine improvement in a semen measurement would not establish that the method selects a male birth.

Anecdotes or an appeal to tradition cannot substitute for clinical evidence about a particular preparation. Both partners should disclose supplements during fertility assessment. If there is a concern about semen quality, use an appropriate evaluation rather than adding an unmeasured combination of roots, seeds and extracts.

Body temperament and genital oil routines

A recommendation to “warm” the body through food or massage is not a demonstrated way to select a boy. Massage chosen for comfort is different from a treatment claimed to influence fertilization. The same distinction applies to oils applied around the abdomen or flanks.

Do not start a genital-oil routine as a sex-selection treatment. Coconut, olive and sesame oils are not proven tools for this purpose, and products used near genital tissue need appropriate safety and compatibility information. If lubrication is needed while trying to conceive, ask about a suitable product rather than assuming a kitchen oil has the desired effect.

What would a credible success rate need to show?

A claim that a method works well but is not guaranteed still needs data. The evidence should explain who followed the programme, who did not, how many pregnancies and births occurred, and whether outcomes were checked consistently. A collection of happy stories does not provide that comparison.

People can have a boy after following a ritual without the ritual causing the outcome. Families with a different result may be less likely to report it, or may be told they followed the rules incorrectly. Neither pattern establishes effectiveness. There is no defensible success percentage to assign to the combined home programme.

IVF and genetic testing are a separate medical discussion

IVF involves medical treatment and laboratory fertilization; embryo testing can be used for particular inherited conditions. It is not simply a more expensive version of a food or timing plan. If a sex-linked condition is the concern, genetic counselling can explain testing that addresses the actual condition.

The availability and permitted uses of embryo testing depend on local rules and clinical circumstances. IVF and testing have costs, burdens and limitations: there may be no suitable embryo for transfer, and transfer does not guarantee a live birth. Ask a licensed service about realistic outcomes rather than accepting a promise of a guaranteed child.

Put preparation and support where they can help

A preconception appointment can review health conditions, medicines, supplements and vaccination needs. CDC advises 400 micrograms of folic acid daily before and during early pregnancy for neural-tube-defect prevention; some people need a different prescribed plan. Folic acid supports pregnancy health, not the choice of a boy or girl.

Ask for fertility advice if conception is taking longer than expected or there is a known concern. If family pressure is making the process distressing, discuss that too. You can decline a costly regimen, an uncomfortable sexual rule or blame about the outcome while still caring deeply about becoming a parent.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Fertility guidance distinguishes opportunities for conception from claims about choosing infant sex. The reviewed evidence does not establish the proposed timing, position, diet or herbal programme as an effective home sex-selection method.

Herbal safety, sodium intake and preconception care need their own evidence. A product can be familiar or culturally important without having a proven effect on the desired outcome. IVF/genetic testing requires an individualized specialist discussion and local eligibility checks.

How BeMama can help

Use a pregnancy-planning appointment to ask about health, medicines and practical support. Bring any product labels or promises that worry you so the actual claim can be reviewed.

When to seek help

Do not increase salt, take concentrated herbal mixtures or use genital products as a sex-selection treatment. Seek clinical advice about symptoms or an exposure; this article does not prescribe a fertility regimen.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A detailed traditional programme does not establish control over infant sex.
  • Ovulation tracking supports conception planning, not reliable boy selection.
  • Salt-loading, herbal courses and genital oils have no justified role as home sex-selection treatment.
  • Semen measurements, pregnancy rates and male-birth rates are different outcomes.
  • Preconception care and genetic counselling address actual health needs.

Frequently asked questions

Will a particular season or weekday help me conceive a boy?

There is no established evidence for that claim. A precise timetable does not make a method scientifically validated.

Does intercourse close to ovulation guarantee a boy?

No. Fertile-window timing and choosing infant sex are different questions. Research has not established a practical timing method for boy selection.

Must I lie on my right side afterward?

No. That is not a proven sex-selection step, and remaining still after sex has no established fertility benefit.

Does orgasm need to happen in a particular order?

No. There is no established sequence that selects a boy. Comfort and mutual agreement matter more than a performance rule.

Should both partners follow the warming-food list?

It is not a validated sex-selection diet for either partner. Familiar foods can be enjoyed without treating a prescribed combination as medicine.

Is sea salt a safer way to follow the plan?

Sea salt still adds sodium. Increasing it offers no established sex-selection benefit and can be harmful to blood-pressure health.

Are herbal teas safe because they are natural?

Not necessarily. The ingredients, concentration, other medicines and possibility of pregnancy all matter. Ask about the actual product rather than relying on the word natural.

Would improving sperm count necessarily make a boy more likely?

No. A semen measurement does not show that a method changes the sex of a resulting child.

Does IVF guarantee a boy and a live birth?

No. Specialist procedures and testing have limits, and permitted uses differ by location. An inherited-condition concern belongs in genetic counselling.

What if I already followed a regimen and am worried?

Keep the product labels and tell a clinician what you used and when. Do not assume harm occurred, but obtain advice about the specific exposure and any symptoms.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
